The respondent, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax in the hands of the respondents under section 34(1) (b) read with section 24B of the Income tax Act. The Income tax Officer held that the amounts received by the heirs and legal representatives of the deceased were not taxable and that the income tax was not liable to be levied under the Act in the year of assessment. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amount received by the respondents was not taxable. The Appellate Tribunal held that the income received by the respondent was not taxable and the section had no application to the case. The High Court in reference held that the sums received by the heir and legal representatives were not taxable. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The question whether a particular amount was income or not had nothing to do with the time of its receipt and the question of receipt was material only for the purpose of determining whether on that amount tax was to be levied. [711 G] The section does not authorise levy of tax on receipts by the legal representatives of a deceased person in the years of assessment succeeding the year of account being the previous year in which such person died. [712 G] The question whether the amounts received were income of the Hindu undivided family or merely represented inheritance or realisations of the assets of the deceased was not a question of law within the meaning of section 24B. [713 G] The liability of the heirs and the legal representatives to pay tax under section 24B(1) is not a question which is covered by the section but is a question which can be referred to the High Court. [714 G] The assessee was keeping accounts on cash basis and he was entitled to deduct the amount from the income tax as if the legal representatives were the assessees and the amount was liable to tax under section 23B(1). [714 A] The assessee had discontinued his profession in the previous year. The income tax Officer was entitled to assess the total income of the deceased person as if the tax was payable by the deceased or any tax which would have been payable under the Act by the deceased if he had not died. [614 E] The assessee 's case was not covered by section 24B and the question whether the amount received was income of the family was not a matter which was covered by the provision of section 24 B. The Tribunal also accepted the workmen 's contention that the minimum wages in the Company should have been fixed at the average level of wages in the other comparable industries in the region. The Tribunal, however, held that the Company was entitled to a higher bonus. The Company contended that the Tribunal committed the error of not making a proper computation. The Company urged that the Tribunal erred in not making a correct computation of the wages in the company 's case and that the Company should be directed to pay the higher bonus. HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the minimum basic wage in so far as it consists of basic wage and dearness allowance should be fixed at the rate of three months basic wage in each case and in no case was the dearness allowance and the production bonus elements of the total wage. The appellant, a Hindu widow, filed a suit for partition of the coparcenary property in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, in which the appellant was the widow, and the respondent, the daughter and the widow, were impleaded as defendants. The appellant filed a suit in the Court for partition of her coparcenary property, claiming a share in the coparcenary property, on the ground that the appellant was not entitled to a share of the property in the coparcenary. The trial court dismissed the suit, but the High Court, in appeal, reversed the decree of the trial court. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit properties belonged to the joint family, that there was no prior partition and that the appellant is entitled to a 7/24th share, and that the respondent is entitled to the share of the appellant. HELD: The appellant 's suit based as it was on the provisions of section 6 of the Hindu Women 's Rights to Property Act, 1955, is essentially a claim to obtain a share in a coparcenary property, and the proviso to that section is attracted. [757 B] The Hindu Succession Act, 1956, is a beneficial legislation, and is intended to provide for the advancement of the interests of the Hindu women, and for the maintenance of the Hindu widow and the daughter, and the daughter and sister in all areas where the Mitakshara law exists. [758 C] The Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929, conferred heirship rights on the son 's daughter, daughter 's daughter and sister, on the surviving members of the coparcenary. [759 D] The Hindu Women ' Rights to Property (Amendment) Ordinance, 1966, conferred heirs ' rights on the sons ' daughter 's son, daughter ' and sister in class I of the Schedule and therefore, by virtue of section 6(1) of the Hindu Succession Act the widow 's daughter ' was entitled to a 1/24th of the share. [760 D] The appellant ' was the widow ' and the daughter 's sister in class II of the Schedule, and the widow ' 's daughter in class II, and the son ' daughter ' in class II. The appellant ' 's suit, based as it is, on the provisions Of section 6(a) of the Act, is essentially of a claim to a share in ' the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death

The appellant was the holder of a large tract of land in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The assessee received a sum of Rs. 36,396/ as compensation for the land revenue of the State. The Income tax Officer, in spite of the objection of the assessee, held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the sum of Rs, 36,396/- was chargeable to tax under the Act as the income was not agricultural income for "although the pension was determined with respect to the quantum of rent collection the rent collections or the land could not be said to be the immediate source of the pension. The High Court, in reference, held that from the language of the letter of July 7, 1837 it was manifest that the right which was conferred was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. The High court, in appeal, held that since the amount of pension was determined by the Income tax Officer in the absence of a specific provision in the letter of the July 7, the right which had been conferred was a personal right to the assessee and could not be a share of the former. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The source of the right in which a fraction of the net income of the trust is to be appropriated by the appellant as his remuneration is not in the right to receive rent or revenue of agricultural lands but rests in the covenant in the deed to receive remuneration for management of the trust. The income of the Trust appropriated by the assessee as remuneration is not income exempt under section 4(3)(viii) of the Income tax Act. [704B] The source of income is clearly the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and, therefore, it is not agricultural income as defined in the Act. The income was not a personal income but was a personal income. The income from the trust appropriated by the appel lant was not income exempt from taxation as agricultural income. [704D] The income of trust appropriated by him as remuneration is neither income nor income. The character of the income appropriated as remuneration is now not the same as the character in which it was received by the appellant. [704E] The source or character of the Income Tax Officer 's order was not the arrangement arrived in 1837 but the source of the income was the arrangement arrived. [704F] The source was not the agreement but the source was the arrangement.

The respondent, a dealer in the business of selling goods, was assessed to sales tax under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, and the tax was assessed on the turnover of the transferee. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the assessment order. The High Court held that Rule 21 A was ultra vires the rule making power of the State Government under section 19(1) and 19(2)(c) of the Act and that the respondent was not liable to pay the sales tax due from his predecessor in title, and that the State Government had no authority under section 19 of the Act to create a legal fiction by which the transferee of the business was constituted as the dealer liable to pay tax in respect of the turnover of transferee. The State Government appealed to this Court. HELD : The word 'assessment ' in the scheme of sales tax and income tax legislation is a term of varying import and import. The word 'assess ' in the rule is used sometimes to mean the computation of income, sometimes the determination of the amount of tax payable, and sometimes the whole procedure laid down in the Income tax Act for imposing liability on the tax payer. [663 C] The word 'Assessment ' in the Madras General Clauses Act, 1904, is a term which is used sometimes, to mean the determination of amount of tax paid by the transferor, but there is no such provision in the Act for the period with which we are concerned in the present case. [664 D] The word "assessment" in the scheme, of sales tax, and income tax Act is a term, of varying import, and import. [665 D] The words "assessment" and "assessment" used in section 19(2) (c) of Act, are used sometimes to denote the computation of the income, sometimes, the determination of tax payable by the transferor. But there is no other provision in the Madras Act which provides for the period within which the provisions of the Act shall come into operation. [666 D] The State Government has no authority under the rule making powers under section 19 (1) and (2) of the Madras General Clause Act, to frame the impugned rule. [667 D]

The appellant company was incorporated in January, 1946 as a private limited company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace & Co. The Tribunal also held that the Tribunal had found that in all the awards in recent years the trend had been to fix the retirement age at 60. [430 A] The Tribunal has not committed any mistake in making the observation that the Tribunal was wrong to disturb the decision of the Tribunal. [430 B]

The appellants were tried and convicted for the offence of dacoity and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The law advises that the presumption of innocence of the accused is not weakened by the fact that the accused was concerned with the crime itself. The presumption is stronger when the discovery of the fruits of crime is made immediately after the crime is committed. The presumption of innocence is greater when the discovery is made immediately before the crime is caused. [742 C] The law advizes that the presumption may be drawn from a piece of evidence which connects him further with the crime. There is then no question of presumption. The evidence strengthens the other evidence already against the accused. [743 E] The law amicus curiae is not correct. If there is other evidence, to connect an accused with the crime, even though small, the finding of the stolen property with him is a piece of paper which connects he further with the murder. The appellant company was a registered firm carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling tea. The appellant contended that r. 5 of the Bombay Village Panchayat Act, 1958, was ultra vires the Act and that the appellant was entitled to the levy of octroi duty. The appellant contended, inter alia, that r. 3(b) did not require that the octroi limits should be fixed in the resolution. Held, that r, 5 of the Rules framed under r. 3 of the Bombay District Panchayat Act, 1961, required the Panchayat to notify to the public not only the proposal about the tax selected by it for levy, but also the rules relating to that tax which must mean the action taken under the Act and the rules. The appellants were the workmen of the appellant No. 1. The conciliation proceedings were held on a complaint by Assistant Commissioner of Labour under section 33 read with section 31 of the Act. The conciliation officer submitted his report and the conciliation officer submitted the report. The appellants were convicted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1) of the Act and sentenced to imprisonment for a period of one year and to pay a fine of Rs. 100/ . The appellants were also convicted under section 33(2) read with s.33(1) and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for one year and a fine of 1/2 months. The appellants filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the legality of the order of the Chief Presidency Magistrate, Bombay, setting aside the order of dismissal and the High Court, reversing the order of acquittal, held that as the conciliation proceedings had continued for a period, the conciliation proceedings could be continued. Held, that the object of conciliation was to get a settlement made with expedition and therefore under section 12(6) of the , the conciliation proceedings must be continued after a fortnight and if proceedings were not closed, the conciliation officer would not have been in a position to submit his report within 14 days. The provisions of the Act were not intended to be a bar to the continuance of the conciliation proceedings. The object of conciliation is to get a dispute resolved by conciliation proceedings and not to terminate the proceedings before the conciliation officer. The object was to get the settlement made with promptitude and to avoid delay. The object being to get a conciliation proceeding completed within a fortnight, the conciliation Officer would not have to submit his reports within 14 days of the commencement of the conciliation proceeding or within such shorter period fixed by the appropriate Government. The provisions Of the Act were intended to be applicable to all conciliation proceedings whether in regard to utility services or otherwise. The object could not be to get a reference to a Court, Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal under section 10 of the Act, as the case may be. The provisions were intended to give protection to the workmen concerned in the dispute, and the termination of the conciliation was deemed to take place when the report of the conciliation officer was received by the appropriate government. The provisions in the Act were meant to give protection against the failure of conciliation proceedings.

The appellants were displaced persons and on 30 8 1952 the respondent entered into an agreement with them, Exhibit C, whereby the mills and the factory in question were leased to the appellants for a period of five years on the terms and conditions set out therein. The appellants were put in possession of the mills and, on 30 8. 1952, the respondent entered in an agreement with the appellants, Exhibit C. The appellants filed a suit against the respondent for a declaration that the lease granted by them was invalid and that the lease was void and that the respondent was liable to be evicted. The suit was dismissed by the trial court and the High Court in appeal. The appellants contended that section 12 of the Act applied only to properties of the evacuee and that the property which had been leased to them was not the property of the evacuee by reason of the sale in favour of the appellants, and that the notice, Exhibit C was ultra vires the powers of the Custodian under that section. Held, that the Custodian had no authority under section 12 of Act XXXI of 1950 to issue any directions with reference thereto. The section was intended to repel a possible contention that section 12 applied only to those properties of the Custodian and not to those of the evacuee. The section expressly authorises the custodian to vary the terms of the lease and that cannot be reconciled with the contention that it confers no authority on him to go back upon his own contracts. The operative portion of the section which confers power on the Custodian to cancel a lease granted by himself and not by the evacuee, is unqualified and absolute and that power cannot be abridged by reference to the provision that it could be exercised only so as to override a bar imposed by any law but not the contract under which the lease is held, and that section 12 did not apply to leases granted by the evacuee.

The appellant, a registered firm, was found carrying on business in Bombay. The firm was assessed to tax under the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876, for the assessment year 1953 57. The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 13 of the Bombay City land Revenue Act, 1887, requiring the assessee to appear before him in person on the 16th June 1955 and to show cause why he should not be apprehended and confined to civil jail in execution of a warrant issued under section 13. The assessee filed a petition under section 13 Of the Act for the issue of a notice of demand on the assessee for payment of the assessed amount of tax. The Income Tax Officer issued a show cause notice on the assessee, and the Additional Collector issued a notice of the demand on the appellant for payment of tax. On the appellant 's failure to appear before the Assistant Collector, the Assistant Collector issued a showcause notice on the appellant. The appellant contended that the notice was violative of article 21 of the Constitution. The appellant 's objection was that the notice could not be said to be violative of article 14 of the Constitution because the notice was not in terms and by itself, it was not a different and alternative mode of recovery of the tax but only confers additional powers on the Collector for the better and more effective application of the only mode of recovery authorised by the body of sub section (2) of section 46. The appellant also contended that the Collector had no jurisdiction to proceed under section 32 of the Act for recovery of the demand of the assessed tax. Held, that the impugned notice was violative, of article 21. The impugned notice was not violative of article 31 of the Constitution and was therefore violative of article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution, because the impugned law was based on a territorial classification having a reasonable nexus or correlation between the basis of classification and the object sought to be achieved by the Act. The impugned law was founded on a territorial class of persons, and the impugned law, was based on an intelligible differentia and the subjection, for the purpose of the recovery of the amount of tax, was not violative Of article 14 of that Constitution. The impugned Act was based on the territorial classification of the State into two categories, namely, (1) that the property in the State was exempt from the levy of the tax and (2) that the tax was not a tax on property but on property. The impugned tax was not on property but was a tax on the property.

The appellant applied to Government for renewal of lease under r, 30 of the Rules framed under the Act. The Government refused to renew the lease. The appellant thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Government. The High Court held that the termination of the appellant 's lease was bad as it did not give three months ' notice to the appellant or provide for any compensation as required by section 20 of the Abolition Act. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The scheme of the Act is to render ineffective all rights created after July 1,1945, for a period beyond one year. The scheme of r. 30 is to render meaningless all rights created by the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition. The scheme is not to render ineffective any rights which were already created after July. 1, 1944, but only void and not void, all that follows is that the Government must do some overt act to terminate the transaction. [563 E] (iv) The scheme was to render ineffective the rights created after the notified date. The second proviso to sub section (1) of section 20(2) of the Act, which provides for compensation for the determination of rights created before the notified date, is not attracted. The scheme was not to render nugatory any rights which had already been created after July l, 1945 but only voidable at the instance of the Government and that being the position, the Government must have some overt act, to terminate the lease and the lessee would also be entitled to compensation under section 20(3).
